claim_text: The process of nitriding [of steels] is conducted at temperatures 500-570°C in an ammonia atmosphere.

caveats.text: The 500-570°C range is standard for gas nitriding specifically. Other nitriding methods (plasma, salt bath) operate at different temperature ranges and atmospheres.

Some authoritative sources give a narrower range of 495-565°C (Neal Systems) or 500-530°C (ScienceDirect), while others extend the upper limit to 580-650°C (Miheu, Thermal Processing Magazine). The 570°C upper bound is a commonly cited textbook value but not universal.
At temperatures above ~560-570°C, the compound layer can become porous due to increased ammonia dissociation and nitrogen supersaturation.
The claim implicitly refers to gas nitriding. Plasma nitriding can operate from 340-590°C, and salt bath nitriding typically at ~570°C using molten cyanide salts rather than ammonia.

sources.title: Neal Systems — Gas Nitriding technical guide
Thermal Processing Magazine — Temperature effect on nitride layers

reason: The 500-570°C range in an ammonia atmosphere is a standard textbook description of gas nitriding of steels, confirmed by multiple independent sources. The range is broadly correct but the upper bound varies across sources (530-650°C depending on specific process conditions).

number_comparison.deviation: Minor — the claim's 570°C upper bound is within the commonly cited range

fragile_points: The 570°C upper limit is not universal — many authoritative sources cite 530°C or 565°C as the practical maximum
The claim does not distinguish between gas nitriding and other nitriding methods
At temperatures approaching 590°C, the Fe-N eutectoid transformation can occur
questions_for_author: Does the claim refer specifically to gas nitriding (ammonia atmosphere) or to nitriding in general?
Is the 570°C upper bound taken from a specific textbook or standard (e.g., Lakhtin's classification)?
